description: Umbra Team is a group of technology and space exploration enthusiasts taking part in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Combining software development, scientific research, data analysis and 3D visualization, we are building UmbraView, an interactive tool that makes lunar mission planning more accessible. It turns complex terrain, lighting and communication data into intuitive visuals that help users compare landing sites, explore mission scenarios and grasp the challenges of returning to the Moon.
summary:
UmbraView is a free web app that shows, for any site near the Moon's south pole and any date, when the Sun and the Earth are above that site's real horizon. 

We build each site's horizon from NASA's LOLA terrain models, compute the Sun and the Earth hour by hour over 30 days from that date, and turn the result into plain answers: whether the Sun and the Earth are up now, when the Sun sets or comes back, how much of the period has sunlight, the longest darkness, when the Earth sets or rises, how much of the period it stays in view, and the landing windows when both are up for at least 24 hours. 

This is what the challenge asks for: comparing sites and dates quickly to judge power (sunlight) and direct-to-Earth communication (Earth in view), without the complex interfaces of specialist tools. At the south pole, a small change in location or date can change whether a mission is feasible, so this comparison needs to take seconds, not hours.
details:
Project Details

What it does and how it works

Near the lunar south pole the Sun stays low, and crater rims and mountains hide it for long stretches. They can also hide the Earth. A lander needs both: sunlight for power and heat, and a line of sight to Earth to communicate. UmbraView shows, for any point on the Moon and any date, when the Sun and the Earth are actually above the surrounding terrain, with full detail near the south pole.

The person picks a site in one of two ways: by clicking on a 3D Moon, or from a list. The list has the IM-2 (Athena) landing site and the centres of the 9 Artemis III candidate regions. The person then sets a date in UTC. For a 30-day period from that date (one full lunar day), the panel shows:

  • whether the Sun and the Earth are in view now, hidden by terrain, or below the horizon;
  • the next sunset (or sunrise) and the share of the period with sunlight;
  • the longest darkness;
  • the next Earthset (or Earthrise) and the share of the period with the Earth in view;
  • the landing windows: stretches of at least 24 hours with at least half of the Sun and part of the Earth in view at the same time.

The screen also shows:

  • the site's sky: its real 360° horizon, with the paths of the Sun and the Earth over the period, solid where they are visible and dashed where the terrain hides them, and a timeline of the period with the landing windows;
  • a landing-area map ("Show landing areas"), which paints every place on the Moon that has a landing window in the chosen period, so sites can be compared at a glance;
  • the 3D Moon with NASA's real colour and terrain, lit by the Sun of the chosen date, with the shadows of the mountains, over the real star field. Near the pole the terrain is shown at true scale;
  • an Earth–Moon–Sun view, not to scale, with the Moon's orbit, the axes and the libration, which explains why the Sun grazes the pole.

Behind it, the app does four things:

  1. Terrain. From the pole to 84°S, it loads only the NASA LOLA terrain tiles around the chosen point (about 0.5 MB): 80 m detail up to 10 km away, and 960 m terrain up to 200 km. Elsewhere on the Moon it uses global LOLA terrain at 1.9 km per pixel (from NASA's CGI Moon Kit), and the panel says the result is approximate.
  2. Horizon. It traces the terrain in 360 directions, out to 200 km, for an observer 2 m above the ground, to build the point's real horizon.
  3. Sun and Earth. It computes their positions hour by hour.
  4. Visibility. It compares them with the horizon to find when each is in view, and when both are.

All of this runs in the browser, with no server. The landing-area map uses horizons computed in advance on a 5 km grid within 84°S and a 2° (61 km) grid elsewhere, and is calculated in a Web Worker.

Benefits

  • Real terrain. The answer comes from the actual terrain, not a flat horizon, so a site in sunlight is not confused with a dark one a few kilometres away.
  • Validated. Near the south pole, we checked our results against NASA's visibility maps (Mazarico et al. 2011). Across 372 points, the mean error is 2.1 to 2.6 percentage points for sunlight and 1.2 to 1.6 for Earth visibility. Our Sun and Earth positions match JPL's SPICE reference to within 0.01°.
  • Easy to use. It is free and needs no installation or account. It also works with the keyboard alone.

Intended impact

We want to make lunar south pole lighting easy to explore. That region is where NASA's Artemis III candidate landing regions are. Exploring LOLA terrain and illumination data usually takes specialist tools and expertise. UmbraView turns the data into a direct answer that a student, a teacher, a journalist or an early-stage mission planner can read in seconds. It shows why the choice of site and date matters. The code is open source (MIT), so others can check, reuse and extend it.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Web app: JavaScript, React, three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei for the 3D scene, and Astronomy Engine for the positions of the Sun and the Earth. It is built with Vite.
    • Vitest and Testing Library for automated tests, including tests of the engine against NASA and JPL values;
    • ESLint, with accessibility rules;
    • GitHub Actions, which runs lint, tests and build on every change.
  • Hardware: our own laptops and desktops. No special hardware is needed: the app adapts its terrain detail to what the computer can handle.

What makes it creative

  • Two conditions, one answer. NASA's polar maps show sunlight and Earth visibility separately, as long-term averages. UmbraView combines the Sun and the Earth, for a specific date, into a single answer: the windows when a lander would have both power and communications.
  • Real horizon, in the browser. UmbraView computes the horizon of any point the person clicks, from NASA terrain, live in the browser. Instead of an average, it gives the hour-by-hour timeline from the chosen date.
  • Where landing is possible, at a glance. The landing-area map applies the same rule to the whole Moon for the chosen date.
  • Full NASA terrain, small downloads. By splitting the terrain into tiles, the app delivers detailed NASA data with a download of about half a megabyte per site.

Factors the team considered

  • Accuracy against download size. We measured how terrain resolution affects the error. Using 160 m or 240 m terrain instead of 80 m raised the mean sunlight error from 2.1 to 3.4 and 5.1 percentage points. The brightest sites, the ones that matter for landing, lost the most. So we kept 80 m and split it into tiles.
  • Area covered. Full detail goes from the pole to 84°S: NASA's original 13 Artemis III candidate regions lie within six degrees of the pole. The rest of the Moon, including the centres of 2 of the current 9 regions, uses the global terrain, and the panel marks the result as approximate.
  • Length of a landing window. We started with 6 days, but that had no mission requirement behind it. In 30 days, only 38% of the sampled points between 85°S and 90°S had a 6-day window, against 58% with 24 hours. We chose 24 hours: a shorter minimum would fill the list with stretches of a few hours.
  • No invented data. Every coordinate, date and name comes from a cited source. Artemis III regions are shown at the centre of the USGS outline and labelled "(center)", so they are not read as official landing points.
    • The app works with the keyboard alone.
    • The Moon stops rotating when the person interacts with it.
    • Motion respects the system's reduced-motion setting.
